arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Hawkins argued Congress did not grant federal courts authority to order consecutive sentences to unimposed state sentences.
Mr. Jay stated the Bureau of Prisons has historically decided where and when sentences are served.
Mr. Young argued the right to impose punishment is judicial and Congress must clearly transfer such authority.
Justice Sotomayor questioned the clarity of the statutory text regarding multiple terms of imprisonment.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of federal sentencing authority under the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984. The core issue is whether Congress granted district courts the power to order federal sentences to run consecutively to state sentences that have not yet been imposed. the side that brought the case argues this authority does not exist.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the boundary between judicial sentencing power and executive prison administration. It determines whether federal judges control the timing of sentences relative to future state convictions. The outcome shapes the balance of power between the judiciary and the Bureau of Prisons. It clarifies the scope of the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984.
